hero.title: Taste Prediction for Small Molecules with Graph Neural Networks
hero.intro: This project uses a graph neural network to estimate, from the structure, how likely a small molecule is to be sweet, bitter, umami or tasteless.
demo.select: Or pick a dairy-related preset molecule
search.label: Search any small molecule

search.fragments: The input has several fragments (for example a sodium salt or hydrochloride); only the largest one was kept.

flow.1.title: Molecule
flow.2.title: Standardize
flow.3.title: Graph
flow.3.sub: atoms are nodes, bonds are edges
flow.4.title: Graph neural network
flow.4.sub: atoms pass information to their neighbors, 3 rounds
flow.5.title: Taste
flow.5.sub: one probability each for sweet, bitter, umami, tasteless
method.data: Data. Two public datasets were merged: ChemTastesDB (main source) and the data released by the VirtuousMultiTaste project. After unifying the labels there are 3,937 organic small molecules: 1,799 sweet, 1,569 bitter, 127 umami and 201 tasteless. When sources disagree about a molecule, the positive record wins (for example, bitter in one source and not bitter in another counts as bitter). Peptides (3 or more amino-acid residues), inorganic salts and molecules with more than 64 heavy atoms were left out.
method.model: Model. The same model design and atom features as this site's odor predictor: each atom is described by its element, number of neighboring atoms and hydrogens, charge, aromaticity and ring membership. After 3 rounds of message passing, the atoms are pooled into one molecule representation and turned into 4 probabilities. The model has about 100,000 parameters and runs directly in your browser.
method.eval: Data split. Molecules with rings were split by ring scaffold into training (80%), validation (10%) and test (10%) sets, so every ring scaffold in the test set is new to the model. Molecules without rings (about 20%) were split at random.
method.explain: Atom contributions. The coloring on the structure uses occlusion: each atom of the molecule (after removing counter-ions and neutralizing charges) is removed in turn, the model is run again, and the change in the taste's probability is recorded. Atoms whose removal lowers the probability (orange) are what the model relies on; atoms whose removal raises it (blue) hold the prediction down. This shows which structures the model weighs, not that they chemically determine the taste.
results.intro: Performance is measured with AUROC: take one random molecule that has a taste and one that does not; AUROC is the chance that the model scores the first one higher. 0.5 is random guessing, 1.0 is perfect. The table shows results on 394 test molecules.
results.note: Graph neural network: mean ± standard deviation over 3 training runs with different random seeds. The baseline describes each molecule with a fingerprint (a code recording which small structural fragments it contains) and predicts with logistic regression.
results.takeaway: The graph neural network performs about as well as the simple fingerprint baseline: the baseline is slightly better for sweet and bitter, the network is better for tasteless (but the test set has only 21 tasteless molecules, so this is uncertain). With data of this size, the more complex model brings no clear advantage.
results.umami: Umami: {n} of the {pos} umami molecules in the test set are nucleotides like inosinate and guanylate, and the test set has no phosphorus-containing molecules that are not umami. Both models score 1.000, which does not show that they can really judge umami. For reference, on the {vpos} phosphorus-free umami molecules of the validation set the network scores {gnn} and the baseline {lr} (the validation set was used for model selection, so this is optimistic).
results.drug: Drug bias: about one in five bitter molecules reached clinical trials according to ChEMBL (mostly drugs, plus a few nutrients such as amino acids), against about 4% of sweet molecules. On the {n} drug molecules in the test set, the network separates bitter from non-bitter with an AUROC of only {drug}, against {nodrug} on non-drugs, and non-bitter drugs are more often predicted as bitter.
results.deployed: These scores come from the model trained on the training split only. After evaluation, the model used on this page was retrained with the same settings on all data to cover more structure types (such as nucleotides). It has no independent test set, so no separate scores are reported for it.
limits.class: Taste categories only. The model does not predict taste intensity, thresholds or relative sweetness, and ignores concentration, temperature and the food matrix.
limits.sour: Sour and salty are not modeled. The data has only 72 sour and 20 salty molecules, and saltiness comes mostly from inorganic salts: not enough to train a reliable model.
limits.bias: Source bias. Drugs make up a large share of the bitter data, so the model may treat "looks like a drug" as a sign of bitterness. Some molecules have a single source record whose label may be wrong (for example, butyric acid and vanillin on this page are recorded as sweet).
limits.peptide: Peptides not included. Peptides with 3 or more amino-acid residues (such as bitter and umami peptides in cheese) are not in the training data, so predictions for them are not reliable. Molecules with more than 64 heavy atoms (such as rebaudioside A) are not supported either.
limits.stereo: No stereochemistry. The model cannot see chirality: D-leucine (sweet) and L-leucine (bitter), or glucose and galactose, look like the same molecule to it.
limits.safety: Not for safety assessment. The model says nothing about toxicity, allergenicity or regulatory status. Bitter does not mean toxic, and sweet does not mean safe.
footer.data: Data: ChemTastesDB v2.1 (Rojas et al., Food Chemistry: Molecular Sciences 4, 100090, 2022; Zenodo, CC BY 4.0); VirtuousMultiTaste (Androutsos et al., npj Science of Food, 2024; GitHub, MIT). The raw data is not redistributed here.
footer.chembl: Drug flags: ChEMBL (EMBL-EBI), used only to assess data bias.
hero.sub: Enter a molecule; a graph neural network estimates whether it is sweet, bitter, umami or tasteless.
footer.short: Data: ChemTastesDB (CC BY 4.0) and VirtuousMultiTaste (MIT). Not for safety assessment. See method & sources.
about.practice: In dairy products I pay most attention to bitterness and to off-tastes that appear unintentionally during optimization. I also look at sweetness and fat-related mouthfeel, such as the effect of lactose on sweetness, bitter peptides from protein hydrolysis, and the effect of fat content on richness. This tool only predicts whether a small molecule is sweet, bitter, umami or tasteless; it is not suitable for peptides and does not cover mouthfeel, which still need sensory evaluation.
